beats.intro: Lesson eight. [[sub]]Why meetings are the manager's medium, and how to run the most valuable one: the one-on-one.
beats.badname: Meetings have a bad name. [[study]]One study found managers spend up to half their time in them, and implied it was wasted. [[druck]]Peter Drucker said more than a quarter was a sign of poor organization. [[whyte]]William Whyte called them labour that contributes nothing. [[grove]]Grove disagrees. Giving know-how and making decisions happen face to face. [[med]]So a meeting is the medium of managerial work. Don't fight it. Use it well.
beats.kinds: There are two kinds. [[proc]]Process-oriented meetings share knowledge and information, on a regular schedule. [[miss]]Mission-oriented meetings solve one problem, often with a decision, and are called as needed. [[reg]]Process meetings should be regular, so people know the format, can batch their business, and can plan the time. [[three]]Intel used three: the one-on-one, the staff meeting, and the operation review.
beats.oneone: A one-on-one is a meeting between a manager and one report. [[teach]]The manager teaches skills and know-how, [[learn]]and the report supplies detail on their work and their worries. [[casual]]People say, I see her several times a day. But a passing chat is not a one-on-one. [[story]]Grove's own began early at Intel. Two of his reports gave him private lessons on memory design and manufacturing. [[pupil]]They prepared like teachers. He took notes like a pupil.
beats.often: How often? [[trm]]It depends on the report's experience with the task at hand, not their age or general experience. Grove calls it task-relevant maturity. [[new]]New to the task: about once a week. [[vet]]A veteran at it: every few weeks. [[pace]]Pace matters too. A fast-moving area like marketing needs more frequent meetings than a quieter research group.
beats.long: How long? [[short]]Would you raise a big problem in a fifteen-minute slot? No. You would stick to easy things. [[hour]]Grove's minimum is an hour. [[where]]And where? In or near the report's own work area. [[clues]]You learn a lot: are they organized, do they hunt for documents, are they constantly interrupted?
beats.theirs: Most important: it is the report's meeting. [[agenda]]They set the agenda and the tone. [[prep]]Someone has to prepare. A manager with eight reports would prepare eight times. Each report prepares once. [[outline]]So the report writes an outline. It forces them to think the issues through, [[pace]]and it lets you pace the meeting by how meaty each item is. [[walk]]They bring the supporting material and walk you through it.
beats.cover: What goes on the agenda? [[ind]]Their indicators, especially the ones signalling trouble. [[since]]Anything important since last time: hiring, people problems, organization, plans. [[pot]]And, very important, potential problems. Even a hunch that something is wrong is worth raising, because it opens a window into the black box. [[nag]]Above all: whatever is nagging at them.
beats.ask: Your role is to get them talking. [[druck]]Drucker put it well: good managers don't talk to their people about their own problems; they get their people to talk about theirs. [[one]]Grove's rule: ask one more question. [[more]]When you think they have said all they want to, ask another. [[bottom]]Keep going until you both feel you have reached the bottom of it.
beats.notes: Both of you should take notes on the outline. [[mind]]It keeps your mind from drifting, and organizes what you hear. [[hand]]And when your report writes down an action, it is a commitment, like a handshake. [[follow]]Your notes let you follow up next time. [[hold]]Keep a hold file, too: non-urgent items saved for the next one-on-one. That is batching, and it cuts down the interruptions.
beats.heart: A one-on-one is the place for heart-to-heart issues. [[q]]Are they happy with their own performance? Is something blocking them? Do they doubt where they are going? [[zing]]But watch for the zinger: a big issue dropped in the last five minutes. I've been looking for another job. [[time]]Make room for it early. [[remote]]Remote one-on-ones work too, with care: the outline in advance, notes on both sides, and notes swapped afterwards.
beats.rolling: Schedule them on a rolling basis. [[fixed]]A fixed slot, like every second Wednesday, collides with a vacation, and the meeting is lost. [[roll]]Instead, book the next one as each one ends, working around what is coming. [[home]]Grove even held one-on-ones at home, over dinner with each of his teenage daughters. Different tone, but each took the other seriously.
beats.lev: Now, leverage. [[mtg]]Ninety minutes, every two weeks. [[work]]It can improve some eighty hours of your report's work, [[you]]and update what you know about it. [[base]]It builds the shared base of information and approach that delegation needs.
beats.teach: And the report teaches you. [[trend]]In one one-on-one, Grove's head of sales walked him through the order trends. [[slow]]Business had stopped growing, and it was not just the summer lull. [[both]]They reached the same conclusion: be cautious about expansion. [[fan]]The sales head scaled back his own plans. Grove passed the conclusion to every group he supervised. One meeting moved them all.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Meetings are the medium of managerial work: process meetings are regular, mission meetings solve one problem. [[w2]]Set one-on-ones by task-relevant maturity, an hour at least, near their desk. [[w3]]It is their meeting: their outline, their worries. [[w4]]Ask one more question, take notes, and keep a hold file. [[w5]]Book the next one as you finish. Now the lesson practice.
